facts.text: The white-faced heron is a pale, slightly bluish-grey bird with yellow legs and white facial markings.
facts.quote: It is a medium-sized heron, pale, slightly bluish-grey, with yellow legs and white facial markings.

facts.text: It will boldly raid suburban fish ponds but flies off on long, slow-beating wings if disturbed.
facts.quote: although it is prompt to depart the scene on long, slow-beating wings if disturbed, it will boldly raid suburban fish ponds.

facts.text: Its most common call is a gravelly croak or gobble, typically given in flight or in aggressive encounters.
facts.quote: The most common call of the white-faced heron is a gravelly croak or gobble, graak or graaw and is typically given in flight, in interactions or in aggressive encounters.

facts.text: A typical clutch has three to five pale blue eggs and incubation lasts approximately 25 days.
facts.quote: A typical clutch has three to five pale blue eggs. with an average size of 48.5×35 mm. Normally only one brood is raised per year. Incubation lasts approximately 25 days.

facts.text: Both parents share building the nest, incubating the eggs and caring for the young.
facts.quote: Both sexes share the task of building the nest, incubating the eggs and caring for the young.

facts.text: It breeds in austral spring, but can breed at other times in response to rainfall.
facts.quote: Breeding generally takes place in the austral spring, but the birds may breed at other times in response to rainfall.

facts.text: The heron turns up everywhere from farm dams and crops to golf courses, beaches and garden fish-ponds.
facts.quote: The white-faced heron is locally nomadic and found in both fresh and salty wetlands, farm dams, pastures, grasslands, crops, shores, saltmarsh, tidal mudflats, boat-harbours, beaches, golf courses, orchards or in garden fish-ponds.

facts.text: It was self-introduced to New Zealand in the late 1940s and is the only heron recorded breeding in Tasmania.
facts.quote: It was self-introduced to New Zealand in the late 1940s. It is the only heron recorded breeding in Tasmania.

facts.text: The Ngarrindjeri people of the Lower Murray region in South Australia knew the white-faced heron as krawli.
facts.quote: The Ngarrindjeri people of the Lower Murray region in South Australia knew it as krawli.
